write.desc: The basic set structure of the real line: neighbourhoods, open sets, limit points, closed sets, closure and interior, and how they behave under complements, unions and intersections. These points belong together because each one is defined from the epsilon-neighbourhood and has an equivalent description using sequences, and the later parts on compactness, connectedness and continuity use both views.

points.name: Epsilon-neighbourhoods and interior points
points.what: The learner can write the epsilon-neighbourhood V_epsilon(a) = (a - epsilon, a + epsilon) = {x : |x - a| < epsilon} and can decide and prove whether a point is an interior point of a set, meaning some neighbourhood of it lies inside the set.
outside: absolute value as distance and inequalities |x - a| < epsilon

points.name: Open sets
points.what: The learner knows that a set is open when every one of its points is an interior point. They can prove from the definition that open intervals, R and the empty set are open, by choosing epsilon as the distance to the nearer endpoint, and that [a,b) is not open because no neighbourhood of a fits inside it.

points.name: Limit points and isolated points
points.what: The learner knows that x is a limit (accumulation) point of A when every neighbourhood of x contains a point of A other than x, and that a point of A that is not a limit point is isolated. They can find the limit points of intervals, Z (none), {1/n} (only 0, which is not in the set) and Q (all of R), with proofs.
outside: density of the rationals and irrationals in R

points.name: Limit points through sequences
points.what: The learner can prove that x is a limit point of A exactly when some sequence in A, with no term equal to x, converges to x. They can build such a sequence by choosing a point in each neighbourhood of radius 1/n, and can switch between the neighbourhood view and the sequence view.
outside: epsilon-N definition of convergence of a sequence
Archimedean property (1/n can be made smaller than any epsilon)

points.name: Closed sets
points.what: The learner knows that a set is closed when it contains all its limit points. They can prove that closed intervals, Z and {1/n : n in N} together with {0} are closed, and that {1/n : n in N} on its own is not closed because it is missing the limit point 0.

points.name: Closed sets through sequences
points.what: The learner can prove that A is closed exactly when the limit of every convergent sequence of points of A is in A. They can use this test to show directly that [a,b] is closed and that (0,1] is not.
outside: limits preserve non-strict inequalities (order limit theorem)

points.name: Open exactly when the complement is closed
points.what: The learner can prove that a set is open exactly when its complement is closed, and can use this duality to turn a question about closedness into one about openness and back.

points.name: Neither and both: open is not the opposite of closed
points.what: The learner understands that a set can be neither open nor closed, as [a,b) and Q are, and can be both, as R and the empty set are, and can prove each claim. They know that R and the empty set are the only subsets of R that are both, which is proved later with connectedness.
outside: density of the rationals and irrationals in R

points.name: Unions and intersections of open sets
points.what: The learner can prove that any union of open sets is open and that a finite intersection of open sets is open (taking the smallest epsilon), and can use (-1/n, 1/n), whose intersection over all n is {0}, to show why an infinite intersection can fail to be open.
outside: unions and intersections of indexed families of sets
Archimedean property (1/n can be made smaller than any epsilon)

points.name: Unions and intersections of closed sets
points.what: The learner can prove, using complements and De Morgan's laws, that any intersection of closed sets is closed and that a finite union of closed sets is closed. They can use [1/n, 1], whose union over all n is (0,1], to show that an infinite union can fail to be closed.
outside: De Morgan's laws for indexed families of sets

points.name: Closure of a set
points.what: The learner knows that the closure of A is A together with its limit points. They can prove that it is closed and that it is the smallest closed set containing A, and can compute closures such as that of (a,b), {1/n} and Q, whose closure is R because Q is dense.
outside: density of the rationals in R

points.name: Interior of a set
points.what: The learner knows that the interior of A is the set of its interior points. They can prove that it is the largest open subset of A, and that the complement of the closure of A is the interior of the complement of A. They can compute examples such as the interior of [a,b] and the interior of Q, which is empty.
